prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "AT&T INC." (ticker T), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "T", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: AT&T Inc.
markets: US wireless (mobile phone and data) service
US home broadband (fiber and fixed wireless)
Business networking and legacy wireline services

mission.statement: Connecting people to greater possibility – with expertise, simplicity, and inspiration.
mission.source: AT&T corporate profile page (att.com, 'Opening the Door to Greater Possibility')
mission.plain: AT&T wants to link people together so they can do more with their lives.

about.plain: AT&T runs one of America's biggest mobile phone networks, so phones can make calls and use the internet. It also lays fiber-optic cables to homes and offices to bring very fast internet. Businesses and police, fire and ambulance teams use its network too. People pay it every month for these services.
about.customers: Families, individuals, businesses and government agencies across the United States (and, until its sale closes, mobile customers in Mexico).
about.everyday: If your phone shows 'AT&T' at the top of the screen or your home Wi-Fi comes from AT&T Fiber, you are using its network.

money.plain: monthly phone plans and the phones themselves
networks, internet and old phone lines for companies

money.part: Home internet and other consumer wireline
money.plain: AT&T Fiber home internet and older home services
phone plans in Mexico (being sold for $2 billion)
home internet sent over its 5G mobile network
phone coverage from space with partner AST SpaceMobile

result.summary: AT&T has a real but narrow advantage: a national wireless network, valuable spectrum licenses and a fiber network passing about 38.6 million locations are very costly to copy, and only three national carriers exist. But wireless is a mature, three-way contest where T-Mobile, Verizon and cable companies compete hard on price, so the advantage protects steady cash flow more than it allows rising prices or fast growth.

pricingPower.evidence: AT&T raised its wireless Administrative & Regulatory Cost Recovery Fee from $3.99 to $4.99 per line from August 5, 2026 (and the business fee from $2.49 to $3.49), and still added 432,000 postpaid phones with 0.86% churn in Q2 2026; but Q4 2025 postpaid phone ARPU fell 0.3% to $56.57 and Q4 2025 churn rose to 0.98% from 0.85%, showing limited room to push prices.

moats.evidence: AT&T is one of the oldest US brands and holds about $129 billion of wireless licenses (June 30, 2026), including 30MHz of 3.45GHz and 20MHz of 600MHz spectrum bought from EchoStar for $23 billion (closed July 2026); the brand itself carries little price premium.

Bundling fiber and wireless (42.5% of AT&T advanced home internet households also take AT&T wireless in Q2 2026), family plans and phone installment plans keep postpaid phone churn under 1% a month, though number portability keeps switching easy.
Phone networks interconnect, so a customer gains nothing from other people being on AT&T rather than a rival.
With 120 million Mobility subscribers and $125.6 billion revenue in 2025 it spreads $22 billion of yearly capital investment widely, but Verizon and T-Mobile have similar scale.
The US supports only three national wireless networks, and in its fiber areas a second fiber overbuilder rarely earns a return, so few new entrants appear.
AT&T is the incumbent; it is more often the target of counter-positioning (cable MVNOs, SpaceX satellite service) than the attacker.
It has long experience building and operating networks, including FirstNet for first responders, but rivals have equal engineering skill.
Spectrum licenses and rights-of-way are scarce, government-allocated assets, and AT&T runs FirstNet under a 25-year federal contract, but rivals also own large spectrum holdings.

customers.evidence: AT&T Fiber ranked #1 in ACSI customer satisfaction for the fourth year in a row (May 2026) and postpaid phone churn was 0.86% in Q2 2026, but wireless churn rose to 0.98% in Q4 2025 and the carrier brand is not loved.

talent.evidence: AT&T had about 133,030 employees at end-2025 (about 43% union-represented), has cut its workforce repeatedly, and is not commonly ranked among top employers.

product.evidence: AT&T Fiber won Ookla's first US 'Best Home Internet' award (February 2026, median 369 Mbps down/309 Mbps up), but in wireless RootMetrics' 1H 2026 overall award went narrowly to Verizon (98.4 vs AT&T 98.3) and T-Mobile is generally faster.

competitors.name: Verizon Communications
competitors.note: National wireless carrier, Fios and Frontier fiber, business networking.

competitors.name: T-Mobile US
competitors.note: National wireless carrier and largest 5G fixed wireless home internet provider.

competitors.name: Comcast (Xfinity, Xfinity Mobile)
competitors.note: Cable broadband against AT&T Fiber, plus fast-growing mobile service on Verizon's network.

competitors.name: Charter Communications (Spectrum, including Cox)
competitors.note: Cable broadband and Spectrum Mobile in many AT&T fiber areas.

competitors.name: SpaceX (Starlink)
competitors.note: Satellite broadband and direct-to-cell service; buying spectrum to push into wireless, cited in Bernstein's October 2026 downgrade.

competitors.name: Lumen Technologies
competitors.note: Enterprise networking and fiber; sold its consumer fiber business to AT&T in February 2026.

competitors.name: Altice USA (Optimum)
competitors.note: Cable broadband and Optimum Mobile in some AT&T areas.

competitors.name: EchoStar (Boost Mobile)
competitors.note: Small wireless brand now reliant on partner networks after selling spectrum to AT&T and SpaceX.

competitors.name: América Movil (Telcel)
competitors.note: Market leader in Mexican wireless, where AT&T is number two until its sale closes.

competitors.name: Cox Communications
competitors.note: Cable broadband, now combined with Charter.

marketShare.market: Share of Q2 2026 US wireless phone/line net additions among the five largest providers (AT&T, Verizon, Comcast, Charter as reported; T-Mobile is a Recon Analytics estimate)

threats: SpaceX/Starlink moving into direct-to-cell wireless with newly bought spectrum (Bernstein downgraded AT&T to Market Perform on October 12, 2026 citing this)
Cable companies (Comcast, Charter) taking a large share of wireless net additions with cheap bundled mobile plans on Verizon's network
Price competition among the three national carriers limiting ARPU growth (Q4 2025 postpaid phone ARPU down 0.3%)
High debt ($144.0 billion at June 30, 2026) after the $23 billion EchoStar spectrum and $5.75 billion Lumen fiber deals, with $23-24 billion of yearly capital investment
Fast decline of legacy wireline revenue (Q2 2026 Legacy revenue down 25.9%)
T-Mobile and Verizon fiber expansion (Verizon closed Frontier in January 2026) eroding AT&T's fiber lead

ceo.name: John Stankey
ceo.background: Loyola Marymount finance BBA (1985), UCLA MBA (1991); joined Pacific Bell in 1985, former AT&T CTO and WarnerMedia CEO; chairman since 2025

c1.evidence: US telecom is mature: AT&T's revenue was $125.6 billion in 2025 versus $120.7 billion in 2022, about 1.3% a year.

c2.evidence: Customers pick AT&T for its fiber (ACSI #1 four years running, Ookla Best Home Internet 2026) and fiber-plus-wireless bundles, but in wireless rivals offer near-identical coverage and service.

c3.evidence: Nearly every American knows the AT&T name and it has 120 million Mobility subscribers, but it is one of three similar carriers rather than the default leader, and carrier brands rarely earn enthusiastic recommendations.

c4.evidence: Its purpose 'Connecting people to greater possibility' is rarely emphasised; management communicates mostly in terms of free cash flow ($18B+ in 2026), buybacks and leverage targets.

c6.evidence: “big phone company, old, reliable, expensive” - people see AT&T as a dependable but unexciting utility with fees and contracts, so the impression is mixed.

c7.evidence: US wireless and broadband is a very large market but grows only low single digits; fiber and AI data-center connectivity are growth pockets rather than a strong secular wave.

c8.evidence: It is expanding fiber to a target of 60 million+ locations by end-2030 and testing satellite-to-phone service with AST SpaceMobile, but these extend its existing business rather than open big new markets, and it is leaving Mexico.

m1.evidence: Stankey has a clear, consistent plan of 'fiber plus 5G' convergence, but it is a focused telecom strategy rather than a vision of a new future.

m2.evidence: Stankey is a career AT&T executive (since Pacific Bell in 1985), not a founder, though he has stuck with a long-term fiber build-out.

m4.evidence: Customer satisfaction in fiber is top-ranked, but Stankey's era includes repeated workforce reductions and a 2021 shareholder rejection of executive pay.

m5.evidence: AT&T's culture is focused on network operations and cost discipline, not on inventing new products and technologies.

m6.evidence: Stankey was AT&T's CTO (2008-2012) and CIO and knows the network well, but his education is in finance and business, not engineering.

m7.evidence: There is no public evidence either way that Stankey's stewardship aims at a purpose beyond running a profitable network business.

m7b.evidence: No commencement speech by Stankey at a top university was found.

m8b.evidence: Stankey is a low-key corporate executive rather than a distinctive public personality.

m9.evidence: Since 2023 he has delivered steady results (2025 adjusted EPS $2.12 vs $1.95, more than 1 million fiber net adds and 1.5 million+ postpaid phone net adds), but he oversaw the WarnerMedia deal that was later unwound and a 2022 dividend cut.

m10.evidence: AT&T runs multi-year cost-cutting programmes and cut capex-heavy legacy copper, but it is not known for a culture of frugality.

c10.evidence: Its network connects about 120 million wireless subscribers and first responders through FirstNet, which matters greatly, but it serves mainly the US and rivals provide the same service.

p2.evidence: Building national 5G and fiber networks costs over $20 billion a year and is vital infrastructure, but two other US carriers do the same.

f1.evidence: Reported revenue fell from $143.1 billion (2020) to $134.0 billion (2021) and $120.7 billion (2022) on divestitures, then rose to $125.6 billion in 2025 with a small dip in 2024.

f2.evidence: Operating margin rose from 5.9% in 2020 to 19.2% in 2025 mainly because big 2020 impairments ($15.7 billion) dropped out, and it was 19.3% in 2021 too, so the underlying trend is flat.

f3.evidence: At June 30, 2026 AT&T had $144.0 billion of debt against $17.6 billion of cash and $40.3 billion of 2025 operating cash flow, though stockholders' equity was positive at $126.4 billion.

f4.evidence: Operating income rose from $8.4 billion (2020) to $24.2 billion (2025) and operating cash flow from continuing operations from $37.5 billion to $40.3 billion, but with a 2022 operating loss along the way.

v1.evidence: AT&T Fiber is arguably the best home internet (Ookla 2026, ACSI #1), but its wireless service is not clearly better than Verizon or T-Mobile.

v2.evidence: AT&T does not appear near the top of major best-places-to-work rankings and has repeatedly cut jobs.

c5.evidence: If AT&T vanished overnight, about 120 million wireless subscribers, 10.4 million fiber customers and FirstNet first responders would lose service until they switched, but rivals could absorb most of them over time.
